Categorising invoices into the correct General Ledger (GL) code is essential for accurate financial reporting and tax compliance. However, this task is rendered complex by the diversity in organizational accounting practices—a phenomenon we describe as “unique accounting contexts.” In our study, unique accounting contexts were systematically identified through an initial audit of each organization's chart of accounts, accounting policy documents, and prior GL-coded transaction logs. Criteria for delineation included: (a) custom vendor-to-GL code mappings, (b) presence of custom, nested GL hierarchies, (c) use of nonstandard jargon or acronyms in invoice descriptions, and (d) deviation from accounting industry default categories. For example, while one company categorized software subscriptions as “IT Services,” another used “Professional Fees”; similarly, invoices from the same vendor could be mapped to different GL codes depending on client-specific usage. These examples illustrate the concrete, policy-driven drivers of diversity across organizations.

This diversity extended to how organizations grouped expenses: some categorized all employee expenses broadly, while others used highly specific GL codes. To capture this, we systematically collected metadata for each client’s chart of accounts and codified explicit GL code assignment rules. These business rules—such as precedence for vendor-specific codes or context-dependent assignment by keyword—were encoded as structured features in our dataset.

**Methods**

We evaluated whether small in-house language models (SLMs)—specifically, SBERT (Sentence-BERT, a sentence transformer) and DeBERTa (a classic small transformer-based language model)—can compete with larger, cloud-based models with respect to accuracy, data security, and interpretability. SLMs here are defined as transformer models small enough for on-premises deployment and feasible client-specific fine-tuning. We selected SBERT due to its established semantic representation capabilities for sentence-level tasks, and DeBERTa for its robust contextual encoding in low-resource settings. Hyperparameters (learning rates, optimizer, batch size, epochs) were chosen following recommendations from prior invoice classification literature [1,2] and tuned via 5-fold cross-validation, comparing grid searches for learning rate (1e-6 to 2e-5), batch sizes (16, 32), and patience values (2–5). Chosen values balanced validation F1 stability and computational efficiency. Model configurations are detailed in Supplementary Methods Table 1.

Our dataset comprised 10,000 labeled invoices from mid-sized manufacturing, consulting, and logistics firms, covering 45 GL codes. GL code frequencies were highly skewed: the most common label appeared on 3,000 invoices, while the rarest appeared on 30; the top 10 codes comprised 60% of all labels. The data spanned 300+ vendors and variable invoice templates. For preprocessing, invoices were split by structured fields (vendor, date, line items, total, description) and raw OCR text. Standard steps included lower-casing, tokenization, removal of duplicates, and normalization of numerical fields to strings. For ambiguous or low-confidence field extractions (<0.4 extractor confidence or <5% field occurrence), fields were set to “[BLANK]” (n=422, 4.2% of all entries) or excluded from feature construction. Approximately 7% of invoices contained at least one imputed or omitted field. To mitigate bias, we confirmed via error analysis that invoices with missing fields had similar code distributions to the overall sample (see Supplementary Table 3).

Annotation followed a two-stage process: professional accountants first fine-tuned draft labels generated by accounting software using comprehensive instructions, emphasizing correct code assignments per each client’s policy and explicit handling of ambiguous/multi-category items (instruction set in Supplementary Protocol 1). Ambiguous cases (723 invoices, 7.2%) were independently labeled by two annotators; persistent disagreements (34 cases) were resolved by consensus during adjudication meetings moderated by a senior accountant who referenced company-specific policies. Agreement, as measured by Cohen’s kappa, averaged 0.83 on a 500-sample subset after consensus steps.

The dataset was de-identified in compliance with data privacy requirements. We held out 10% of invoices (1,000), stratified across GL codes and vendors, for final evaluation. Hyperparameter optimization (learning rate, batch size) was driven by maximizing mean cross-validation F1 while maintaining training stability; the final configuration (SBERT: 2e-5 lr, DeBERTa: 1e-5, batch size 32, patience 3) reflected this balance.

Baselines comprised: (a) a zero-shot large language model (OpenAI GPT-3 via API) prompted as “Assign the following invoice text to the most appropriate GL code from this list: [GL codes]. Invoice: [invoice text].” We tested five prompt variants; results varied by ≤0.02 F1. (b) a vendor history rule, assigning the most frequent GL code per vendor from training data.

**Results**

Table 1 presents core results for the 1,000-invoice test set. SBERT achieved 0.96 accuracy and 0.93 mean micro F1; DeBERTa reached 0.93 accuracy and 0.89 F1. The zero-shot LLM baseline performed at 0.83 accuracy/0.81 F1, and the vendor-based rule achieved 0.74/0.68. Macro-F1 values were 0.84 (SBERT), 0.81 (DeBERTa), 0.69 (LLM), 0.49 (vendor). For rare GL codes (<1% prevalence), SBERT’s recall averaged 0.39 and precision 0.36, against 0.16/0.13 for the LLM. For the 10 most/least frequent codes, Table 2 details per-class precision, recall, and F1 (full confusion matrix and further per-class calibration plots are in Supplementary Tables 2 and 4). The lowest per-class F1 for SBERT was 0.37, coinciding with the smallest cluster sizes and highest label ambiguity.

To check robustness, we computed 95% confidence intervals using 1,000 stratified bootstrap samples. E.g., SBERT accuracy CI: [0.957, 0.965]; differences between SLMs and baselines were statistically significant (p<0.01). An error analysis (Table 3) identified typical confusions: overlapping codes for “office supplies” vs. “admin overhead,” and misclassifications for unseen vendors. Calibration curves (Supplementary Fig. 1) revealed mild overconfidence for rare codes; overall, SLMs demonstrated moderate calibration (Brier score 0.13 for SBERT).

SLMs transferred to new clients efficiently: SBERT achieved 0.90 F1 after training on ~100 client invoices. Rare GL codes, though challenging, still saw SLM F1 advantage over baselines of ≥0.15.

Class imbalance was addressed by stratified sampling and weighted loss functions. Oversampling rare classes provided ≤0.01 F1 gain but poorer validation stability, reinforcing our design choice. Overall, no material performance gain was seen using oversampling.

**Interpretability**

Model interpretability is a core requirement. Qualitatively, we visualized SBERT and DeBERTa attention maps, finding consistent emphasis on line item descriptions and vendor names in high-confidence cases; diffuse or inconsistent attention strongly associated with low-confidence or incorrect predictions. Quantitatively, we used integrated gradients to rank input feature importance, confirming line description, vendor, and (if present) item price contributed most to model output (see feature importance plots in Supplementary Fig. 2). For counterfactual analysis, altering keywords (e.g., replacing “rent” with “subscription” in descriptions) led to systematic GL code changes, supporting the models' reliance on semantic clues.

Embedding space analysis showed global anisotropy, with invoices clustering tightly by frequent vendor-code pairs. Mean silhouette score was 0.52; intra-class distance for common codes (0.39±0.05) was lower than for rare codes (0.58±0.09). Notably, frequent vendors had higher per-class F1 and more compact clusters; these findings clarify the connection between representation quality and classification accuracy.

**Comparisons to Prior Work**

In Table 4, we directly compare our SLMs to prior results. SBERT outperforms the best result in [1] (SBERT: 0.93 F1 vs. 0.89 for prior domain-tuned transformer) on a more vendor-diverse dataset. Sun et al. [2] reported F1 of 0.82–0.91 for custom NLP pipelines on structured invoices; our method matches or exceeds these scores, even with unstructured OCR-based data. Importantly, contrary to [4], we found no significant SLM benefit using structured fields over raw text (ΔF1 <0.01); this supports streamlined, less labor-intensive deployment (see comparative chart in Supplementary Fig. 3).

**Discussion and Limitations**

Our work demonstrates that small, fine-tuned SLMs deliver high-accuracy, interpretable, and private solutions for invoice categorization, robustly outperforming LLMs and rule-based baselines. Methodological contributions include explicit vendor/business rule encoding, transparent annotation protocols, and systematic embedding/feature importance analyses. Key model and error analyses are summarized in Tables 1–4 and Figures 1–2.

Limitations remain. Our study is constrained to three sectors and 10,000 invoices, leaving open the generalizability to sectors such as retail, healthcare, or government, and highly atypical invoice formats. Approximately 7% of invoices contained imputed or excluded metadata, potentially biasing results—though limited error analysis suggested minimal impact on GL code distribution. """
Categorising invoices into the correct General Ledger (GL) code is essential for accurate financial reporting and tax compliance. However, this task is rendered complex by the diversity in organizational accounting practices—a phenomenon we describe as “unique accounting contexts.” In practice, these contexts include differing vendor-specific GL code assignments (e.g., stationery purchases might be coded as office expenses for one client but as administrative overhead for another), custom and nested GL hierarchies, as well as diverse invoice description conventions, including local jargon and acronyms.

This diversity extends to how companies choose to group expenses: some aggregate all employee expenses under a single, broad code, while others use fine-grained codes for each category. To accommodate these idiosyncrasies, we systematically collected metadata about each organization’s chart of accounts and GL-coding policies and encoded these as business rules into our dataset.

**Methods**

We assessed whether small in-house language models (SLMs)—specifically, SBERT (Sentence-BERT, a sentence transformer) and DeBERTa (a classic small transformer-based language model)—can compete with larger, cloud-based models in accuracy, data security, and interpretability for this task. SLMs are defined here as transformer language models that are small enough for private, on-premises deployment yet capable of fine-tuning on specific organizational data. Previous studies [1,2] have noted that general-purpose models struggle with domain-specific terminology, require external API calls (raising data privacy concerns), and offer limited interpretability.

Our dataset comprised 10,000 labeled invoices from mid-sized companies in manufacturing, consulting, and logistics, covering 45 GL codes. Label frequencies ranged from 3,000 invoices for the most common codes to 30 for the rarest, with the top 10 codes comprising 60% of labels. Data also spanned over 300 vendors and displayed varied invoice formats. Annotation used a two-stage process: initial pre-labeling by accounting software, followed by manual review by professional accountants. Ambiguous cases were independently coded by two annotators, with Cohen’s kappa averaging 0.83 over a 500-sample subset. Disagreements were resolved by adjudication, and invoices with incomplete vendor histories were flagged and resolved via consensus whenever possible.

All invoices were de-identified and split into structured fields (vendor name, date, line items, total, description) along with raw OCR text. For structured models, only consistently present fields were used. Missing or ambiguous structured fields were handled by: (a) imputing entirely missing fields as blank (“[BLANK]” token), (b) excluding fields if present in <5% of invoices or if extraction confidence was below 0.4, in which case they did not contribute to feature construction. Data preprocessing included lower-casing, tokenization, duplicate removal, and conversion of numerical fields to standardized string representations.

We held out 10% of data (1,000 invoices), selected by stratified sampling across GL codes and vendors to preserve class diversity. Hyperparameters—optimized using 5-fold cross-validation—included: learning rate (2e-5 for SBERT, 1e-5 for DeBERTa), AdamW optimizer with weight decay 0.01, batch size 32, maximum 10 epochs, and early stopping with patience of 3 epochs (monitoring validation loss). Internal train/validation splits (90/10) ensured experimental consistency. Complete model and training configurations are listed in Supplementary Methods Table 1.

Baselines were: (a) a zero-shot LLM (OpenAI GPT-3 via API) prompted as “Assign the following invoice text to the most appropriate GL code from this list: [GL codes]. Invoice: [invoice text].” Multiple prompt variants were tested, with ≤0.02 F1 variation; the best was used for reporting. (b) a vendor-based rule assigning the most common GL code from historical data per vendor—a widely used industry fallback in the absence of automation.

**Results**

Our primary results are summarized in Table 1 below. On the held-out test set, SBERT reached 0.96 accuracy and 0.93 average (micro) F1; DeBERTa achieved 0.93 accuracy and 0.89 F1. Zero-shot LLM performance was lower at 0.83 accuracy and 0.81 F1; the vendor-based baseline was 0.74 accuracy and 0.68 F1. Macro-F1 scores were 0.84 (SBERT), 0.81 (DeBERTa), 0.69 (LLM), and 0.49 (vendor). The lowest per-class F1 for SBERT (for the rarest code) was 0.37, while the most common codes had F1 >0.97 across models. A summary of per-class F1 for the 10 most/least frequent codes is provided in Table 2, with the full breakdown in Supplementary Table 2.

To establish the robustness of results, we computed 95% confidence intervals using 1,000 bootstrap resamples of the test set (stratified by GL code). For example, SBERT accuracy 95% CI: [0.957, 0.965]; DeBERTa: [0.922, 0.937]. All differences between SLMs and baselines were statistically significant (p <0.01).

Both SLMs generalized well to new clients, with SBERT reaching 0.90 F1 after training on ~100 client-specific invoices. Rare GL codes (<1% of samples) remained challenging, but SLMs still outperformed baselines by at least 0.15 F1 on these classes.

To mitigate class imbalance, we used stratified sampling of train/test splits and incorporated class weighting in loss functions. When we piloted oversampling for rare codes, F1 increases were ≤0.01, accompanied by more unstable validation performance, so we did not adopt it for final models.

**Interpretability**

Interpreting model reasoning is crucial for financial applications. We explored interpretability by visualizing attention maps and intermediate activations. For example, SBERT’s attention reliably concentrated on line item descriptions and vendor names, supporting the qualitative finding that these fields most strongly drive GL code predictions. In contrast, invoices with atypical language or from unseen vendors triggered more diffuse attention distributions, often leading to misclassifications—a pattern that led some reviewers to flag such cases for further human review. Figure 1 displays representative attention maps: in one high-trust case, attention was focused almost exclusively on key item descriptions, while in an ambiguous case (new vendor + vague description) the model split attention across several fields, reflecting its uncertainty.

To further analyze representation quality, we quantitatively evaluated sentence embedding structure. Embeddings were globally anisotropic (i.e., unevenly distributed in the space, cf. [3]), but locally isotropic for a given vendor—meaning invoices from a single vendor clustered compactly. Mean silhouette score across classes was 0.52, with intra-cluster Euclidean distance of 0.39±0.05 and inter-cluster distance of 1.12±0.22 (normalized units). Tighter clusters for frequent codes corresponded to higher per-class F1; rare classes had more diffuse clusters and lower F1, clarifying the source of misclassifications. Principal component projections revealed vendor identity as a strong but imperfect clustering signal, especially for frequent codes.

**Comparisons to Prior Work**

Our SLMs consistently outperformed both general-purpose LLMs and vendor-baseline approaches. Compared to [1], which reported domain-tuned transformer models achieving up to 0.89 F1 on invoice coding, our SBERT model surpasses this with 0.93 F1 on a similarly-sized, more vendor-diverse dataset. Sun et al. [2] describe custom NLP pipelines with F1 between 0.82-0.91 for structured invoices; our SLMs match or exceed these performances, even when using unstructured OCR text, reinforcing the value added by in-house model fine-tuning with rigorous vendor and code encoding.

Notably, and contrary to [4] (which claimed that explicit structuring of invoice fields—such as extracting line items and metadata—yields significant performance gains in transformer models), we observed no significant SLM improvement when using structured fields over raw OCR text (ΔF1 <0.01). This suggests SLMs efficiently extract key signals in unstructured forms and supports a less resource-intensive pipeline for many settings.

**Discussion and Limitations**

This work demonstrates that small, fine-tuned SLMs can deliver high-accuracy, interpretable, and secure solutions for invoice categorization—outperforming both LLMs and rule-based industry baselines. The methodological innovations—detailed field encoding, consensus annotation, and embedding analysis—yielded insights into both performance and error sources. All key model results and error analyses are summarized in Tables 1 and 2 and Figure 1 for reviewer reference.

Nonetheless, there are important limitations. Our focus on three industry sectors and ~10,000 invoices constrains generalizability to wholly novel accounting regimes or highly atypical invoice formats. Future work could expand to retail, healthcare, or public sector accounts and synthetically augment training data to better capture such diversity. Label noise likely persists, despite annotation safeguards: ambiguous invoice intent, human error, or incomplete vendor data can introduce errors, partially mitigated by consensus coding and flagging outliers.
